status: CANDIDATE SPEC — FIXED-COUNT EXCHANGE TO SEPARATE SELECTION FROM COUNT; NO ARM, NO RUN, NO TARGET, NO GRANT
question: Does the identity of the served edges move the 16-tag level over and above how many edges are served?
definition: A three-arm fixed-count exchange at the committed cap: identity control, probability-order swap, and a cap-shift calibration that prices one served edge, with the contrast reported in edge-equivalents.
method: The design and its power are computed from committed artifacts only: the cap-response slope gives the level per served edge, the committed cap-112 trace gives the exchange size, and the within-block SD gives the seed-level noise. No arm is run.

arms.must: reproduce the committed level for the seed, or the seed is void

arms.change: transition ordering replaced by the probability-only order
arms.must: serve the same number of candidate edges as arm I

arms.change: prediction cap moved by a few transition slots
arms.must: move the served count without touching the candidate set

refusals: arm S serves a different number of candidate edges than arm I — the swap leaked into the count and the seed cannot separate them
arm I does not reproduce the committed level for the seed
arm C does not move the served count, so the yardstick is missing
the candidate set differs between arms
controls: arm I is the determinism control: an identical configuration must return an identical level
arm C is the yardstick control: a count change of known size must move the level by its edge-equivalent
a sham swap that re-applies the committed order must return the arm I level
design.reporting: contrast in edge-equivalents, with the per-edge rate measured in-run by arm C

decision_rule.statistic: level(arm S) minus level(arm I), divided by the level per served edge measured by arm C, reported in edge-equivalents
decision_rule.supported: at least 2.0 edge-equivalents with an interval excluding zero
decision_rule.otherwise: undecided — the exchange neither separates nor excludes
decision_rule.seed_rule: a seed contributes only if its arms serve the same count; the block is void if arm I misses the committed level

prediction.count_only: the swap moves the level by 0 edge-equivalents
prediction.selection_identity: the swap moves the level by the exchanged edges' worth, about 6.1 edges, with the sign of the edges it adds

reading: The test is a **fixed-count exchange**: run the committed configuration twice on the same seeds — once unchanged (**arm I**) and once with the transition ordering replaced by the probability-only order (**arm S**) — at the same cap and on the same candidate set, so the served count is fixed by construction and only the identity of the served edges moves. A third arm (**arm C**) moves the cap by a few slots to price one served edge in the same conditions, so the contrast is reported in **edge-equivalents** rather than in offset units only this analysis can read. The committed traces already say how big the exchange is: the two orders disagree on **6.1** of **58** served edges per seed (**10.5%**). If identity matters with the same exchange rate the count has, that is **0.1128** coverage units, or **2.60** seed standard deviations of the level — **6 seeds per arm and block** to see it at a 5% two-sided test with 80% power. The decision rule is pre-committed in edge-equivalents: selection identity is **supported** only if the swap moves the level by at least **2.0** edges' worth with an interval excluding zero, **refuted** if it moves by less than **0.5**, and otherwise undecided. The calibration is the point: arm C makes a one-edge effect measurable, so a null in arm S says that swapping **6.1** edges changed nothing a single edge would have changed, not merely that the level was noisy. The design is asymmetric and that is its weakness: **0** seeds per arm and block would be needed to refute a **0.5**-edge effect, against **6** to see the full swap, so the test can support the selection account cheaply but can only fail to find a small identity effect — a null leaves the question open rather than closing it.
limits: The exchange rate is read from the frozen cap curve, which attributes the whole cap slope to the count; the cap also buys window depth, so the per-edge value is an upper proxy until arm C measures it in-run.
Arm S changes the ordering basis, which is an engine-behaviour change: the spec is a proposal that needs a grant, not a thing this analysis may run.
The swap fraction is measured on the committed ordering trace at cap 112 and will not transfer exactly to a block whose candidate pool differs.
Three arms multiply the run cost: the design is only worth mounting if a positive arm-S result would change the selection architecture rather than add another diagnostic.
not_evidence: A specification and a design estimate. It runs no arm, opens no database, measures no level, and is not a treatment, target, freeze, grant or A1 cell.
